rationale: B wins because it finds the pressure point a real reporter would stab first: “Whatnot says it hit $3B in live-auction sales. It won't say what sellers actually make.” A is competent, but its lead angle, “Whatnot's $3B Milestone Tests Whether Live Auctions Have Crossed the US Mainstream,” still accepts the company’s preferred frame before interrogating it. B is meaner in the useful way: it tells the founder which numbers will get challenged before the founder wanders into a reporter call underdressed.
gaps_in_A: “The $3B GMV” quietly converts “annual livestream-commerce sales” into GMV; that may be right, but the update does not state the accounting definition, and the set itself later warns this distinction must be clarified.
“someone who goes live repeatedly each week selling trading cards or sneakers as a primary income source” invents the full-time-seller color the update explicitly does not provide.
“Poshmark, Depop, and eBay — platforms that don't have a live-auction format to counter with” is overconfident competitive analysis without support in the supplied facts.
“The $3B GMV gives a reporter a concrete, dateable benchmark for the story the press has been circling since TikTok Shop's US launch” imports an external peg not present in the update.
gaps_in_B: “A private company with $3B in sales and a $5B valuation is worth less than one times revenue it doesn't keep” is the one bad swing: the math is muddy, and it calls a gross sales number revenue while warning not to do exactly that.
“the shutdown-and-retreat cycle of Western live-shopping efforts” may be true market context, but it is not in the supplied update and needs proof before it becomes pitch copy.
“the top 1% of sellers make the number look like an economy” is a sharp question, but it flirts with implying concentration data that has not been supplied.
“sales figure that funds the argument that it can work” is loose phrasing; $3B supports an argument, it does not prove category expansion is funded or successful.
